hook: Agents are only as good as their tools. **Descriptions drive selection, validation blocks chaos, errors teach recovery.** Tool design IS agent design.

scenes.title: The description IS the API — **to the model**
scenes.sub: Models choose tools by reading, so write for a reader
scenes.narration: A model selects tools the way a developer reads documentation: by scanning names and descriptions. The tool name is the headline — search-documents beats tool-1; verb-noun, specific, unambiguous against sibling tools. The description answers three questions: what does it do, when should it be used, when should it NOT be used — that third one prevents the classic failure of the model grabbing a plausible-but-wrong tool. Argument descriptions matter equally: 'query' needs 'a standalone search phrase, not a question' — the model copies patterns from descriptions into its arguments. Sparse descriptions don't just under-document a tool; they randomize the agent's behavior.

scenes.title: One tool, two descriptions — watch behavior change
annot: The 'Do NOT use for…' clause is load-bearing — it's how you steer the model away from plausible-but-wrong choices
Examples inside argument descriptions get copied — 'refund policy enterprise' will appear in real queries
Defaults in the schema are behavioral guardrails: most calls will leave top_k at 5 unless reason says otherwise
scenes.narration: Read it as marketing copy aimed at a very literal reader. Every sentence changes behavior: the when-to-use boundary prevents tool confusion; the negative clause prevents the near-miss; the example phrase becomes a template the model imitates; the default nudges most calls to sane values. Now the anti-pattern: forty tools with one-line descriptions — the model's tool choice becomes a coin flip, and every flip is a potential wasted loop. Quality-in, quality-out applies with unusual directness here: the model literally receives your documentation as its only interface to the world. Write tool docs the way you'd write a public API's docs — because to the agent, that's exactly what they are.

scenes.title: Never trust LLM-generated arguments — **validate everything**
scenes.sub: The model proposes; your code disposes
scenes.narration: Tool arguments come from a language model — an eloquent guesser, not a guarantee. Treat every call like user input from an untrusted source, because functionally it is. Schema validation is the floor: types, required fields, enums, ranges — Pydantic models mirroring the JSON schema, applied before ANY execution. Business validation is the real gate: can this user access this record? Is this amount within limits? Does this file path escape the allowed directory? A validated argument can still be a catastrophic action — 'delete_file' with a perfectly typed, fully validated path to the production database. Validation stops malformed calls; AUTHORIZATION stops malicious or catastrophic ones. The model proposes, your code disposes.

items.s: Pydantic types, ranges, enums — malformed args rejected before execution
Ownership, limits, allow-listed paths — validated shape ≠ permitted action
Invalid args → error observation back to the model, NOT silent coercion

scenes.narration: Fail-closed deserves emphasis: when validation rejects arguments, return the error to the model as an observation — 'amount must be positive, got -500' — because AG-01's loop can then self-correct. What's forbidden is SILENT coercion — auto-fixing a bad argument and executing anyway; you lose the audit trail and teach the model its sloppiness is free. Layer the checks: schema first — cheap, mechanical; authorization second — user-scoped, policy-driven; rate and blast-radius limits third — 'no single agent run may modify more than N records'. Each layer is one line of defense the model cannot talk its way past, because none of them reads the model's reasoning — they only see its proposed action.

scenes.title: Write errors the model can **act on**
scenes.sub: An error message is an API to the agent's next decision
scenes.narration: In agent systems, an error message isn't written for a human on-call — it's written for the model that will read it in the next loop iteration and decide what to do. 'Error: invalid input' is a dead end: the model has nothing to work with and will guess — usually by retrying identically, forever. An actionable error says: what went wrong, what would make it right. Compare: 'HTTP 404' versus 'No document found for id DOC-123 — check the id format: DOC-<year>-<seq> like DOC-2026-0041'. The second turns a failure into a fixable observation; the agent corrects the id format and succeeds on the next loop. Error design is the difference between an agent that recovers and one that loops.

cards.s: "Error: invalid input" · model has zero information → retries identically or hallucinates a fix
"user_id must be UUID, got '42'. Example: 9f2c…" · model self-corrects next loop

scenes.narration: Test your error messages with one question: 'if I were the model reading this, would I know what to try next?' That reframe produces a style guide: state the constraint that was violated, show the received value, give a correct example, and suggest the nearest alternative when one exists — 'no results for X; the closest matches are Y and Z'. Also distinguish RETRYABLE from terminal in the message itself: 'rate limited, retry in 30s' invites a retry; 'permission denied for user U on record R' should stop the loop, and saying so prevents doomed attempts. Errors are the feedback channel of the agent loop — design them with the same care as the happy path.

scenes.title: Idempotent tools, parallel calls, and the **too-many-tools** wall
scenes.sub: The advanced mechanics that separate demo agents from durable ones
scenes.narration: Three mechanics that decide whether tools survive production. IDEMPOTENCY: agents retry — after errors, after confusion — so tools must be safe to repeat: prefer create-with-client-id over blind create; delete-checking-existence over delete-assuming. An agent that retries a non-idempotent 'charge_customer' twice is an incident. PARALLELISM: independent tool calls should run concurrently — asyncio.gather, PY-10 — not sequentially; agents that fetch five sources one at a time waste fivefold latency. TOO MANY TOOLS: beyond roughly a dozen, selection accuracy degrades — group tools, merge related ones, or let the agent discover tools in layers rather than seeing all forty at once. Tool count is a context problem as much as a selection problem.

items.s: Same call twice = same end state · retries become free
gather() over independent tools · never serialize what doesn't depend
~12+ tools → group/merge/layer discovery · selection accuracy and context both degrade

scenes.narration: The unifying principle: design for the agent's actual runtime conditions — retries, parallelism budgets, limited attention — not for the clean demo path. Idempotency check: run every tool twice in tests; if the second run throws or duplicates, redesign the semantics — upsert, ensure-exists, delete-if-present. Parallelism check: when you see the model emit several independent calls in one turn, execute them concurrently and return all results — most modern APIs support parallel tool calls natively. Tool-count strategy when you genuinely have many capabilities: tool groups exposed progressively — 'search tools' first, deeper tools unlocked by context — mirrors how you'd onboard a human. Tools are the agent's organs; keep them few, safe, fast, and legible.

scenes.title: Custom tools done. What about the powers models bring built-in?
scenes.next: Reel 43 · Built-in Capabilities — code execution, web search, computer use

recap: Tool selection is reading: names, when/when-not descriptions, and argument examples directly shape agent behavior
Validate like untrusted input: schema + authorization + blast-radius limits; fail closed with actionable errors returned to the loop
Idempotent tools make retries safe; parallelize independent calls; keep the tool set small or layer its discovery

quiz.q: Why does a tool description need a 'when NOT to use' clause?
opts: Without it, the model can't distinguish similar tools and picks plausible-but-wrong ones — negative boundaries steer selection
quiz.why: Models disambiguate tools by reading boundaries; a description that only says what a tool does leaves the choice to similarity luck.

quiz.q: What makes an error message 'actionable' for an agent loop?
opts: It says what failed, what constraint was violated, and what a correct attempt looks like — so the model can fix it next iteration
quiz.why: The error is the feedback channel: with a constraint, the received value, and an example, self-correction replaces blind retrying.

quiz.q: Why must agent-facing tools be idempotent?
opts: Agents retry after errors and confusion — a tool that isn't safe to repeat can execute a dangerous action twice
quiz.why: Retries are intrinsic to agent loops; idempotency converts 'the agent got confused' from an incident into a non-event.

code.title: A production-grade tool: validated, idempotent, self-explaining errors
code.body:
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from typing import Literal

class SearchDocs(BaseModel):
    query: str = Field(min_length=2, max_length=200,
                       description="standalone keywords, not a question")
    top_k: int = Field(default=5, ge=1, le=10)
    date_after: str | None = Field(
        default=None, pattern=r"^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$")

def search_documents(args: SearchDocs, user: User):
    if not user.can_search:
        raise ToolError("permission denied: search requires the 'kb' role")
    try:
        hits = vdb.search(embed(args.query), k=args.top_k,
                          where={"acl": {"$in": user.groups}})
    except IndexUnavailable:
        raise ToolError("search index temporarily unavailable — "
                        "retry in ~30s or answer from general knowledge")
    if not hits:
        raise ToolError(
            f"no results for '{args.query}'. Try broader keywords "
            "(e.g. drop qualifiers) or a date filter reset.")
    return [{"id": h.id, "snippet": h.text[:300]} for h in hits]

# Note: ToolError messages are written FOR THE MODEL — constraints,
# received values, next steps. They are the loop's feedback signal.
annot: Pydantic IS the schema gate — the same model serializes to the function-calling schema the model sees
Every failure path raises ToolError with a next action — no dead ends anywhere in this function
The ACL filter rides INSIDE the retrieval — the model never sees chunks the user can't (GA-17's rule)

notes:
# Tool Design

## Schemas & descriptions
- Name = verb_noun, unambiguous. Description answers: what / when / when NOT.
- Argument descriptions carry examples — models imitate them.
- Defaults are behavioral guardrails.

## Validation
- LLM args = untrusted input: Pydantic schema + authorization + blast-radius limits.
- Fail closed: invalid → actionable ToolError back to the loop; never silently coerce.

## Errors the model can fix
- Constraint + received value + correct example (+ nearest alternatives).
- Distinguish retryable vs terminal in the message.

## Craft
- Idempotent tools → retries safe (upsert/ensure/delete-if-present).
- Parallelize independent calls (gather).
- ~12+ tools → group/merge/layer discovery.
